question: How are the six faces of the plot die divided?
choices: Two blank, two Opportunity, two Complication
Three blank, two Opportunity, one Complication
One blank, three Opportunity, two Complication
Two blank, one Opportunity, three Complication
explanation: The plot die is split evenly: two blank faces, two Opportunity faces and two Complication faces. On a normal d6 stand-in, 1–2 are Complications, 3–4 blank, 5–6 Opportunities.

question: When the plot die comes up as a Complication, what upside does the roller get?
choices: Nothing — Complications are purely negative
They add the number on the Complication symbol (+2 or +4) to that d20 roll
They may reroll the d20 once
They recover 1 focus
explanation: A plot-die Complication also adds a bonus equal to the number on the symbol (+2 or +4) to the current d20 roll, so a Complication can actually help the test succeed.

question: Which statement about raising the stakes is correct?
choices: The GM may raise the stakes after seeing the d20 result
Stakes can be raised up to twice on a very important test
Stakes can be raised only once per test and only before the d20 is rolled
Only players can raise the stakes; the GM merely approves
explanation: Raising the stakes happens once per test at most, and it must be decided before the d20 is rolled — never after.

question: A natural 1 on the d20 gives a Complication. How does it differ from a plot-die Complication?
choices: It grants no bonus to the test
It grants a +4 bonus instead of +2
It automatically fails the test
It cannot be spent by the GM
explanation: Complications from the d20's Complication range (a natural 1 by default) don't come with the +2/+4 bonus that plot-die Complications provide.

question: A talent expands your Opportunity range by 2 for a skill. Which natural d20 results now grant an Opportunity on that skill?
choices: 20 only
20–22 (i.e. you need 2 less on the die)
explanation: Expanding the Opportunity range lowers its starting number. The default range is 20 alone, so expanding it by 2 makes it 18 through 20.

question: Which of these is NOT one of the standard ways to spend an Opportunity?
choices: Give an ally's next test an advantage
Recover 1 focus
Turn a hit into a critical hit on an attack test
Recover 1 Investiture
explanation: The standard Opportunity spends are Aid an Ally (advantage on an ally's next test), Collect Yourself (recover 1 focus), Critically Hit (attack tests only) and Influence the Narrative. Recovering Investiture isn't one of them.

question: Which of these is one of the GM's standard ways to spend a Complication?
choices: The roller takes 1d4 damage
The next test made by a PC gains a disadvantage
The roller loses their next reaction
The roller loses 1 Investiture
explanation: The standard Complication spends are Hinder an Ally (the next PC test gains a disadvantage), Become Distracted (lose 1 focus) and Influence the Narrative.

question: Do NPCs normally roll the plot die on their tests?
choices: Yes, whenever a PC would
Only bosses and Fused
Generally no
Only when a PC raises the stakes against them
explanation: The plot die is a tool for PC tests during tense moments; NPC tests generally don't use it.
verify: NPC tests don’t generally use the plot die

question: An ability lets a character with a 25-foot movement rate move half their movement. How far can they move?
choices: 12 feet
12.5 feet
13 feet
15 feet
explanation: Unless a rule says otherwise, you always round down when dividing, so half of 25 is 12.

question: As a general rule, when do two similar effects NOT stack on the same target?
choices: When they come from the same character
When they share the same name
When they both grant bonuses to defenses
When either one has a duration
explanation: Similar effects generally stack unless they share the same name.
verify: unless the effects share the same name

question: A talent's text contradicts a general rule in the core mechanics. Which applies?
choices: The general rule, since it's foundational
The talent's specific rule
Whichever is more favorable to the PC
Neither — the GM must make a skill test
explanation: Specific beats general: when a talent, power or item contradicts a general rule, the specific rule wins (and the GM has final say on any uncertainty).

question: Normally, how many reactions can a character use between each of their turns?
choices: None
One
Two
As many as they have focus for
explanation: A character typically gets one reaction between each of their turns, used when a specific trigger occurs.
verify: one reaction between each of your turns

question: The stakes are raised on a PC's Athletics test. They roll a natural 20 on the d20 and an Opportunity on the plot die. What do they get?
choices: One Opportunity — duplicates merge
Two Opportunities
One Opportunity plus a +4 bonus
A critical success, which replaces Opportunities
explanation: A natural 20 grants an Opportunity even when the plot die is also rolled, so the PC can end up with two Opportunities on the same test.

question: A PC with an advantage rolls two d20s for a Stealth test and gets a 1 and a 16. They use the 16. Do they gain a Complication?
choices: Yes — any natural 1 rolled adds a Complication
Yes, but it grants no bonus
No — only the d20 chosen for the test can add an Opportunity or Complication
No — advantages cancel Complications
explanation: When rolling multiple d20s, a die only adds an Opportunity or Complication if its result is the one chosen for the test. The unused 1 has no effect.

question: A PC benefits from two effects with the same name, each saying it expands their Opportunity range by 2 on this test. Which natural rolls grant an Opportunity?
choices: 20 only
explanation: Range expansions stack only when they come from effects with different names. Two same-named effects count once, so the range is 18–20.
verify: only if they come from effects with different names

question: A player spends an Opportunity to influence the narrative, but you (the GM) think their proposed effect isn't possible. What do the rules say happens?
choices: The Opportunity is lost
The player must accept a Complication instead
You have final say; you can work out a different narrative effect together, or the player picks another Opportunity effect
The player rolls a d20 against DC 15 to force it
explanation: The GM has the final say on narrative Opportunity effects. If one isn't approved, the table can agree on a new narrative effect or the player can choose a different Opportunity effect.
verify: the GM has the final say
